ethiopia.summary: Sudan's army-aligned government has rejected Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed's call for an inclusive dialogue aimed at resolving the ongoing conflict in Sudan. In contrast, a rival administration aligned with the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) has welcomed the initiative, indicating a split in Sudanese factions regarding Ethiopia's role in peace efforts. Abiy's proposal, made on November 24, emphasized the need for a dialogue free from political agendas, aiming to foster national consensus and establish a unity government. However, the army-aligned government accused Ethiopia of bias, alleging it supports the RSF and has facilitated drone operations against Sudan. This rejection comes amid escalating diplomatic tensions, including mutual consulate closures and accusations of foreign drone strikes. The RSF-aligned Transitional Peace Government expressed readiness to engage with Ethiopia's initiative, viewing it as a chance to address the war's root causes and pursue sustainable peace. The situation remains complex, with ongoing allegations and deteriorating relations between Sudan and Ethiopia. (157 words)

ethiopia.title: Proximity, Precedent, and Pragmatism in Ethiopia’s Sudan Mediation Bid - horn review
ethiopia.content: Proximity, Precedent, and Pragmatism in Ethiopia’s Sudan Mediation Bid – HORN REVIEW Home Research and Analysis Ethiopia and the World Horn Geopolitics Global Politics Publications Horn Review Journal Articles Policy Briefs The Greater Horn: Monthly Strategic Brief Horn Review Magazine Weekly Geopolitical Report Research Paper Commentary Event Flagship Events Conferences Brainstorming Sessions Team About Us Contact Us Search Home Research and Analysis Ethiopia and the World Horn Geopolitics Global Politics Publications Horn Review Journal Articles Policy Briefs The Greater Horn: Monthly Strategic Brief Horn Review Magazine Weekly Geopolitical Report Research Paper Commentary Event Flagship Events Conferences Brainstorming Sessions Team About Us Contact Us 2026-11-25 Proximity, Precedent, and Pragmatism in Ethiopia’s Sudan Mediation Bid 0 Comments Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed’s invitation issued on 24 November 2026 to all Sudanese military, political, and civilian actors to convene an inclusive dialogue in Addis Ababa, represents a consequential diplomatic intervention aimed at putting at rest a devastating war now in its fourth year. With humanitarian assessments estimating the death toll above 200,000 and the country enduring the world’s most acute hunger and displacement crises, the initiative warrants serious engagement. Few regional actors, if any, possess the geographic proximity, institutional history, and direct structural stake that Ethiopia brings to the Sudanese crisis, making its proposal a credible mechanism for de-escalation. The framework outlined by Addis Ababa rests upon four interconnected pillars. First, it establishes a structured facilitation process designed to create the political conditions necessary for a durable ceasefire and national consensus. Second, it defines a clear political end-state in the form of a broadly accepted national unity government mandated to restore state institutions, safeguard territorial sovereignty, and reconstruct critical infrastructure. Third, the proposal anchors its legitimacy in Sudanese ownership and Ethiopian equidistance, explicitly prioritizing the preservation of the Sudanese state over the triumph of any single faction. Fourth, it leverages Ethiopia’s regional and international diplomatic networks to build external consensus around a cessation of hostilities and the expansion of humanitarian access. Ethiopia’s credibility as a mediator is rooted in an extensive record of regional conflict resolution. The 1972 Addis Ababa Agreement terminated Sudan’s first civil war, while the 2011 Abyei arrangements and the September 2012 security and oil accords between Khartoum and Juba were similarly brokered in the Ethiopian capital under African Union auspices. More recently, in 2019, Ethiopia operated alongside the African Union to guide the Transitional Military Council and the Forces of Freedom and Change toward the constitutional declaration following the ouster of Omar al-Bashir. That precedent retains significant currency among Sudanese political actors, as evidenced by the Civil Democratic Alliance, known as Somoud, explicitly referencing the 2019 mediation in welcoming the current outreach. The Horn of Africa’s broader diplomatic history reinforces the logic of a regionally anchored settlement. During the Somali crisis, Ethiopia hosted the 1993 Addis Ababa reconciliation conferences and the 1997 Sodere conference before intervening militarily in 2006 against the Islamic Courts Union at the request of the internationally recognized Transitional Federal Government and with diplomatic and intelligence support from the United States. While critics characterized that intervention as partisan, the subsequent political trajectory demonstrated that durable stability in the Horn requires inclusive political bargaining rather than unilateral military victory. Ethiopia remained deeply invested as the political process widened, culminating in the 2008 Djibouti Agreement and the 2009 election of former Islamic Courts Union chairman Sharif Sheikh Ahmed to the presidency, a settlement that succeeded precisely because it integrated former adversaries. Because Addis Ababa treats neighboring state collapse as an existential security concern and possesses decades of institutional experience navigating entrenched factionalism, it is far better positioned to convene Sudan’s rivals than distant capitals whose engagement remains episodic. The Sudanese Armed Forces leadership under Abdel Fattah al-Burhan has nonetheless rejected the initiative , alleging that Ethiopia compromised its neutrality by permitting the Rapid Support Forces to launch drone strikes from Ethiopian territory. Port Sudan has further demanded that the African Union exclude Addis Ababa from any mediation framework, insisting that the venue and agenda remain strictly under Sudanese control. These assertions require rigorous scrutiny. Port Sudan’s accusations regarding cross-border drone launches remain independently unverified, and they occur alongside reciprocal allegations from Addis Ababa regarding Khartoum’s backing of armed factions operating in Ethiopia. More fundamentally, unresolved allegations between neighbors are precisely what regional diplomatic mechanisms are designed to address, rather than grounds for a belligerent party to pre-emptively veto a mediation venue. Moreover, the SAF’s institutional standing to dictate African Union diplomacy is fundamentally compromised. The African Union suspended Sudan’s membership on 27 October 2021, two days after the military coup led by al-Burhan, and the Peace and Security Council reaffirmed that suspension in February 2026 under the African Charter on Democracy, Elections and Governance. Following a Council delegation’s August 2026 assessment that al-Burhan’s administration derives from an unconstitutional takeover, Sudan remained barred from the 39th African Union summit for a fifth consecutive year. An authority whose legitimacy is rejected by the continental body lacks the standing to demand the exclusion of an active member state from a peace process that aligns with the Union’s core mandate. While the SAF retains administrative control over certain territories and occupies Sudan’s seat at the United Nations, de facto control confers the status of a conflict party rather than the sovereign authority to veto diplomatic venues. The SAF’s posture also reflects external geopolitical alignments that diverge from Sudan’s long-term national interests. Cairo has invested substantial political and material capital in the SAF camp, and al-Burhan’s reflexive opposition to Addis Ababa is widely interpreted as deference to Egyptian regional preferences. A leadership prioritizing Sudanese recovery would explore every viable avenue to halt the war, particularly a hosted dialogue that imposes no cost on Sudanese sovereignty. By contrast, Ethiopia possesses an enduring structural stake in Sudanese stability, bound by a shared border, the Blue Nile basin, interconnected borderland communities, and decades of reciprocal refugee flow as Prime Minister Abiy noted in the statement made public. This structural interdependence is most visible in the hydro-politics of the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam. While Sudan stands to gain substantially from regulated water flows, flood mitigation, and power generation, its legitimate technical concerns regarding downstream dam operations can be effectively managed through bilateral mechanisms or the Nile Basin Initiative. Egypt, conversely, views the project through a zero-sum security lens rooted in colonial-era water treaties. Al-Burhan would commit a strategic error by subordinating his long-term basin interests to short-term military and political backing from Cairo. The same calculus applies to the Al-Fashaga borderlands, where recurring friction over fertile territory disputed under colonial boundary demarcations is far better resolved through bilateral diplomacy than weaponized for tactical leverage. The positive reception of Ethiopia’s invitation by the Somoud civilian coalition and the RSF-aligned Transitional Peace Government under the Tasis alliance demonstrates that major stakeholders across the divide view Addis Ababa as a viable venue. Somoud commended Ethiopia’s commitment to Sudanese territorial unity, while Tasis spokesman Khaled Ahmed Danna affirmed the administration’s readiness to engage. Crucially, the principle of parity must apply equally to all belligerents, as neither Tasis nor the SAF holds the unilateral right to dictate preconditions for the other. Consequently, the dialogue should proceed with all willing participants while keeping the process open to those currently abstaining. Admittedly, the timing of the initiative invites critique, as it arrives amidst intensifying military escalation when an earlier bilateral intervention might have constrained the conflict’s trajectory. Previously, Addis Ababa largely deferred to multilateral frameworks such as the Quintet and the Quad, while maintaining that a durable settlement required genuine Sudanese ownership rather than an externally imposed formula. As those multilateral tracks deadlocked amid competing external rivalries and civilian suffering reached catastrophic levels, however, continued diplomatic deference became untenable, making a direct, neighbor-led intervention far preferable to prolonged inaction. Ultimately, the efficacy of the Addis Ababa process will depend on the composition of the negotiating table and the durability of its institutional backing. The dialogue cannot be monopolized by the two primary armed factions. Sudanese civilian coalitions, women’s organizations, youth movements, and civil society bear the heaviest burden of the conflict and possess the strongest mandate for democratic governance, making their substantive inclusion indispensable to preventing a purely transactional elite pact. Simultaneously, Addis Ababa should consolidate its diplomatic role by appointing a dedicated special envoy for Sudan. Given that Ethiopia’s national security is structurally tied to stability across its borders, it requires diplomatic representation at least commensurate with the special envoys maintained by distant European and international powers. Such an envoy would ensure continuous shuttle diplomacy, prepare technical consultations, and sustain momentum between formal sessions. Backed by a dedicated envoy and an inclusive civilian mandate, Ethiopia is uniquely positioned to leverage its historical ties and play a decisive, constructive role in ending Sudan’s war. November 25, 2026 Proximity, Precedent, and Pragmatism in Ethiopia’s Sudan Mediation Bid
ethiopia.summary: Ethiopia's Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed has initiated a significant diplomatic effort to mediate the ongoing conflict in Sudan, which has resulted in over 200,000 deaths and severe humanitarian crises. On November 24, 2026, he invited Sudanese military, political, and civilian actors to engage in an inclusive dialogue in Addis Ababa. Ethiopia's geographical proximity and historical involvement in Sudanese affairs lend credibility to its mediation proposal, which is structured around four key pillars: facilitating a ceasefire, establishing a national unity government, ensuring Sudanese ownership of the process, and leveraging diplomatic networks for external support. Despite the Sudanese Armed Forces' rejection of the initiative, citing concerns over Ethiopia's neutrality, major Sudanese factions have expressed willingness to engage. The success of this mediation will depend on the inclusion of diverse stakeholders, particularly civil society groups, and the appointment of a dedicated Ethiopian envoy to sustain diplomatic efforts. Ethiopia's longstanding commitment to regional stability positions it uniquely to address Sudan's crisis.

ethiopia.title: Ethiopia Vows Direct Role in Shaping Red Sea Security Architecture, Maritime Governance
ethiopia.content: Ethiopia Vows Direct Role in Shaping Red Sea Security Architecture, Maritime Governance - allAfrica.com AllAfrica English (current) En Français Toggle navigation My Account Toggle navigation AllAfrica My Account English (current) En Français Ethiopia Vows Direct Role in Shaping Red Sea Security Architecture, Maritime Governance 25 November 2026 Ethiopian News Agency (Addis Ababa) Addis Ababa — Red Sea security is an integral part of Ethiopia's national security, and the country will continue to play a direct and constructive role in regional maritime governance, Chief of Staff at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, Ambassador Adam Tesfaye, said. The two-day fifth edition of the Horn Dialogue Series is underway in Addis Ababa under the theme: "Re-collaborating Regionalism in the Horn of Africa: Building Strategic Trust, Regional Agency, and Cooperative Interdependence." Opening the dialogue series, Ambassador Adam described the Horn Dialogue Series as an important platform that brings together scholars, diplomats, and other stakeholders to exchange views on pressing regional issues and explore solutions to shared challenges. He pointed out that the Horn of Africa is among the world's most strategically significant regions, with considerable potential for economic growth, supported by its geographical proximity and strong economic and social ties among countries in the region. Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn However, he said the region continues to face multiple challenges. The ambassador pointed out that this geopolitically significant part of the world continues to face multiple challenges, including interstate tensions, internal conflicts, competing national priorities, differing security perceptions, and shifting regional alliances. According to him, these challenges cannot be addressed through individual efforts, stressing the need for coordinated regional responses to economic, social, traditional, transnational, and maritime security concerns. He stated that regional integration remains essential to addressing the region's multifaceted challenges, although translating shared interests in peace, stability, economic development, and connectivity into concrete collective action remains a major challenge. Adam reaffirmed Ethiopia's commitment to regional and continental integration. He further noted that the government firmly believes economic integration serves the best interests of the peoples of the region. He also emphasized Ethiopia's efforts to strengthen regional connectivity through investments in transport and energy infrastructure, as well as its active engagement in regional peace and security initiatives within the frameworks of the Intergovernmental Authority on Development (IGAD), the African Union (AU), and the United Nations (UN). Addressing maritime security, Ambassador Adam underscored the strategic importance of the Red Sea to regional stability, reiterating that its security is directly linked to Ethiopia's national security. In this regard, Ethiopia will continue to play a direct and constructive role in Red Sea governance while pursuing secure and reliable access to the sea through peaceful dialogue, diplomacy, international law, and mutual benefit, he noted. "We strongly believe that Red Sea security plays a pivotal role in the security of our region and is an integral part of Ethiopia's national security," he said. He reiterated that Ethiopia would continue to play a direct and constructive role in Red Sea governance, stressing that such an approach would contribute to advancing peace, prosperity, and strategic cooperation across the region. For his part, Gizachew Asrat, Chief of Staff at the Institute of Foreign Affairs, highlighted the region's critical position linking the Red Sea, the Gulf of Aden, and the Indian Ocean. He stressed that persistent trust deficits and fragmented cooperation have prevented Horn nations from fully capitalizing on their geographical proximity. "The central question is how we can transform the Horn of Africa from a region characterized by geopolitical competition into one defined by shared interests and economic complementarities," Gizachew said. Paul-Simon Handy, Regional Director for East Africa and Representative to the AU at the Institute for Security Studies (ISS), traced the evolution of the dialogue series since its inception in Djibouti in 2022, noting that the fifth edition convenes at a critical juncture marked by renewed regional instability. Handy explained that this year's panels are structured around three core pillars: fostering strategic trust among neighbors with competing interests, asserting regional agency so external actors do not dictate the Horn's security agenda, and advancing "cooperative interdependence" even when political relations remain strained. Jan-Ole Voss, Director of the Konrad Adenauer Stiftung (KAS) Regional Programme Security Dialogue for East Africa, underscored that sustainable solutions must be locally driven rather than externally imposed. "The future of the Horn will ultimately be decided and determined by the countries and peoples of the region," Voss said, noting that recalibrating regionalism means building upon existing AU and IGAD frameworks rather than replacing them. Reaffirming Germany and the European Union's support for multilateral dialogue in the region, he added that trust cannot be built overnight but develops gradually through transparency, predictability, and sustained engagement. ethiopia.summary: Ethiopia has reaffirmed its commitment to playing a direct role in shaping the security architecture and maritime governance of the Red Sea, which it considers integral to its national security. During the fifth edition of the Horn Dialogue Series in Addis Ababa, Ambassador Adam Tesfaye emphasized the importance of regional cooperation to address challenges such as interstate tensions and internal conflicts. He highlighted the strategic significance of the Horn of Africa, advocating for coordinated responses to economic, social, and security issues. Ethiopia aims to enhance regional connectivity through investments in infrastructure and active participation in peace initiatives under the frameworks of IGAD, AU, and UN. The dialogue series aims to foster strategic trust and cooperative interdependence among Horn nations, with experts stressing the need for locally driven solutions to ensure sustainable regional stability. The discussions reflect a critical juncture for the region, marked by renewed instability and the necessity for collaborative efforts to transform geopolitical competition into shared economic interests. ethiopia.title: Ethiopia Showcases Africa's Potential Through Tangible Milestones in Health Sector
ethiopia.content: Africa: Ethiopia Showcases Africa's Potential Through Tangible Milestones in Health Sector - allAfrica.com AllAfrica English (current) En Français Toggle navigation My Account Toggle navigation AllAfrica My Account English (current) En Français Africa: Ethiopia Showcases Africa's Potential Through Tangible Milestones in Health Sector 25 November 2026 Ethiopian News Agency (Addis Ababa) Addis Ababa — Ethiopia is demonstrating Africa's capabilities and potential through tangible achievements and transformative progress in the healthcare sector, Minister of Health Dr. Mekdes Daba said. Speaking to ENA on the sidelines of the 5th International Conference on Public Health in Africa (CPHIA 2026), currently underway at the Addis International Convention Center with more than 30,000 participants from over 100 countries, Dr. Mekdes highlighted the strong multisectoral engagement and high-level participation at the event. She noted that, alongside health officials, more than 46 ministers representing finance, planning, agriculture, and environmental protection are also attending the conference. The Minister emphasized that conference delegates have had the opportunity to witness firsthand Ethiopia's impactful initiatives, proven best practices, and far-reaching transformations across other key development sectors. Follow us on WhatsApp | LinkedIn for the latest headlines She explained that these achievements stand as tangible evidence of the nation's capacity to translate ambitions into concrete results, significantly strengthening international confidence in Africa's potential. Through this collaborative platform, which brings together government and non-governmental institutions, development partners, and the private sector, Ethiopia is also showcasing its scientific and technological advancements across multiple areas, Dr. Mekdes noted. In particular, participants have witnessed the country's pioneering work in artificial intelligence, digital health, primary healthcare, and medical referral systems. The practical application of the Electronic Community Health Information System (eCHIS), an innovative digital platform that enables Health Extension Workers to efficiently monitor, track, and manage community health services, was also among the advancements showcased to delegates. As a result, several countries have expressed keen interest in adopting Ethiopia's healthcare models and digital solutions, creating new opportunities for knowledge exchange, cooperation, and the sharing of best practices. Addressing the evolving dynamics of global health governance, the Minister highlighted Ethiopia's strategic use of health diplomacy to strengthen Africa's voice, influence, and standing on the international stage. She affirmed that the conference will help translate the vision of Africa's health sovereignty into concrete actions and meaningful resolutions. ethiopia.title: Obasanjo to Chair Sasakawa Africa Association's 40th Anniversary Symposium in Addis Ababa
ethiopia.content: Africa: Obasanjo to Chair Sasakawa Africa Association's 40th Anniversary Symposium in Addis Ababa - allAfrica.com AllAfrica English (current) En Français Toggle navigation My Account Toggle navigation AllAfrica My Account English (current) En Français Africa: Obasanjo to Chair Sasakawa Africa Association's 40th Anniversary Symposium in Addis Ababa 25 November 2026 Nile Post (Kampala) By Kenneth Kazibwe Former Nigerian President Olusegun Obasanjo is set to chair the Sasakawa Africa Association's (SAA) 40th anniversary symposium scheduled for December 1-2, 2026, in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia, bringing together African leaders, policymakers, agricultural experts and development partners to discuss the future of the continent's food and nutrition security. The two-day symposium, organised by SAA with longstanding support from The Nippon Foundation, will reflect on four decades of agricultural transformation while exploring innovative strategies and partnerships to strengthen Africa's agrifood systems. Held under the theme "Reimagining Africa's Food and Nutrition Security," the gathering will bring together regional leaders, farmers, researchers, policymakers, private-sector representatives and development partners to examine progress made in agricultural development and identify opportunities for building resilient and sustainable food systems. Obasanjo, a former member of the SAA Board, will chair the symposium, drawing on his longstanding advocacy for agricultural development and agribusiness as key drivers of economic growth, employment creation and food security. Follow us on WhatsApp | LinkedIn for the latest headlines In an earlier interview with SAA, the former Nigerian leader underscored the importance of food security to national stability, describing it as a fundamental pillar of security and development. "For any country in Africa, food security is next to personal security," Obasanjo said. He also highlighted the importance of developing agribusiness across the entire agricultural value chain, arguing that its contribution extends beyond farming and food production to include land preparation, agricultural equipment, processing, distribution and delivery of food to consumers. According to Obasanjo, strengthening agribusiness presents significant opportunities for employment creation, wealth generation and improved food and nutrition security across Africa. The symposium will feature high-level policy discussions and practical exchanges focusing on agricultural extension, climate resilience, food and nutrition security, investment, innovation and the development of inclusive agricultural value chains. Established in 1986 through the shared vision of Japanese philanthropist Ryoichi Sasakawa, Nobel Peace Prize laureate Dr Norman E. Borlaug and former United States President Jimmy Carter, SAA has spent four decades supporting agricultural development and improving the livelihoods of smallholder farmers across Africa. The organisation has operated in 17 African countries, working to strengthen agricultural extension systems, promote improved farming practices and connect farmers and other agricultural value-chain actors to knowledge, technologies and markets. A key component of its work is the Sasakawa Africa Fund for Extension Education (SAFE), which partners with African universities and agricultural colleges to develop practical, demand-driven degree and diploma programmes for mid-career agricultural extension professionals. SAFE currently operates in Ethiopia, Mali, Nigeria and Uganda, with support from The Nippon Foundation, alongside other development partners, donors and collaborating institutions. The 40th anniversary symposium will also showcase success stories from SAA's country programmes, lessons from its agricultural interventions and experiences of young agrifood entrepreneurs, highlighting opportunities to expand the participation of the next generation in Africa's agricultural transformation. A commemorative exhibition titled "40 Years of Walking with the Farmer" will showcase the organisation's four-decade journey through farmer success stories, agricultural innovations and milestones achieved across its country programmes. The strategy focuses on building climate-resilient and sustainable agrifood systems, expanding inclusive markets and agribusiness opportunities, and advancing access to safe, adequate and nutritious food. The anniversary gathering is expected to provide an opportunity for African agricultural stakeholders and international development partners to reflect on lessons from the past four decades while strengthening collaboration towards a more productive, inclusive and food-secure continent. Offers to Host Inclusive Dialogue to End Sudan’s War The Ethiopian prime minister reaffirmed his country's support for Sudan's unity, territorial integrity and stability, saying peace in Sudan was closely linked to security across the Horn of Africa. G Garowe Online 25 Nov 2026 · 15:04 · 2 min read Abiy Ahmed, the prime minister of Ethiopia ADDIS ABABA, Ethiopia — Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed has invited Sudan’s military, political and civilian groups to participate in an inclusive national dialogue hosted and facilitated by Ethiopia, as his government seeks to help end the war that has devastated the neighboring country. In a statement issued in Arabic, Abiy said Ethiopia was proposing a new initiative to bring together all Sudanese parties for comprehensive talks aimed at ending hostilities and establishing a path toward lasting peace. “At this critical historical juncture, the Ethiopian government is putting forward a sincere and genuine initiative calling on all Sudanese parties, across their military, political, and civilian components, to participate in a comprehensive and open Sudanese dialogue to be hosted and facilitated by Ethiopia,” he said. Abiy described the conflict, which erupted on April 15, 2023, as more than a political and security crisis, saying it had become a humanitarian tragedy with consequences extending beyond Sudan’s borders and threatening stability across the region. He said Ethiopia's historical, cultural and people-to-people ties with Sudan made the conflict particularly concerning for Ethiopians, describing the Sudanese as a brotherly people whose suffering resonated deeply with their neighbors. The Ethiopian prime minister reaffirmed his country's support for Sudan's unity, territorial integrity and stability, saying peace in Sudan was closely linked to security across the Horn of Africa. Abiy also recalled Ethiopia's diplomatic involvement during Sudan's political transition in 2019, when Addis Ababa sought to bring civilian and military leaders closer together and support efforts toward civilian rule. He said the latest initiative was intended to provide a neutral and inclusive platform where Sudanese stakeholders could address their differences through dialogue and political consensus. The proposed talks would seek to end the fighting, bridge political and military divisions and establish arrangements for a broader political transition, including the formation of a national unity government with wide support. Abiy stressed that Ethiopia's initiative was not designed to advance a particular political agenda or favor any of the parties involved in the conflict. He said his government was prepared to maintain equal distance from all sides and facilitate credible and respectful discussions. He added that Sudanese people must determine their country's future through their own national will, warning that solutions imposed from outside would not deliver sustainable peace. The war in Sudan has pitted the Sudanese army against the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces, triggering a major humanitarian crisis and forcing millions of people from their homes. The conflict has also raised concerns among neighboring countries over regional security and the growing displacement of civilians. Abiy did not announce a date for the proposed dialogue or specify whether the Sudanese parties had accepted the invitation. ethiopia.summary: Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed has proposed hosting an inclusive national dialogue to help end the ongoing conflict in Sudan, which began on April 15, 2023. In a statement, he emphasized the importance of peace in Sudan for the stability of the Horn of Africa and invited all Sudanese military, political, and civilian groups to participate in the talks. Abiy described the conflict as a humanitarian tragedy with far-reaching consequences, highlighting Ethiopia's historical ties with Sudan and its commitment to supporting the country's unity and territorial integrity. The initiative aims to create a neutral platform for Sudanese stakeholders to address their differences and work towards a national unity government. Abiy stressed that the dialogue would not favor any party and that the future of Sudan should be determined by its people, warning against externally imposed solutions. No date has been set for the proposed talks, and it remains unclear if Sudanese parties have accepted the invitation.

During 17–23 November, rain was reported at only four stations: Banderbeyla (28.3 mm in 2 rainy days), Mogadishu (9.7 mm), Qansax Dheere (1.3 mm) and Cadale (0.8 mm). Satellite estimates (IMERG, 18–24 November) indicate 8–13 mm over parts of Lower Juba and less than 1 mm over the river catchments in Ethiopia. Seasonal totals are almost unchanged after the dry week. By 23 November, 37 stations, 33 of them with a Deyr normal above 15 mm, had already received their full Deyr normal, including Baidoa (405.5 mm, 176% of the Deyr normal), Galkacyo (253.5 mm, 390%) and Banderbeyla (126.7 mm, 316%), which recorded the highest weekly total. Mogadishu rose to 35% of its Deyr normal, while Borama (16%), Burao (21%) and Luuq (25%) remain far below normal. River levels on both rivers are falling or easing and remain well below flood-risk levels. Belet Weyne fell from 3.76 m on 18 November to 3.00 m today, 3.50 m below its moderate flood-risk level. Bulo Burti (2.16 m), Dollow (2.32 m) and Luuq (2.34 m) are also falling, and Jowhar (3.30 m) is easing after reaching 3.50 m on 23 November. Flood water in Jowhar district continues to recede. Satellite images show about 46 km² of flood water in Jowhar district down from about 55 km² last week. Radio Ergo callers (12–18 November) reported river flooding on farms in Jowhar, while many callers in Galgaduud, Bay, the Juba valley and Gedo welcomed the rains Report details Primary country Somalia Source Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations Disaster Somalia: Drought - 2015-2026 Format Situation Report Theme Agriculture Disaster types Drought Flood Language English Share Share this on Facebook Share this on X Post this on LinkedIn Share report link Latest Updates Haiti MSF teams treating alarming numbers of women for sexual violence in Port-au-Prince Format News and Press Release Source MSF Posted 26 Nov 2026 Originally published 25 Nov 2026 Bolivia Bolivia Drought El Niño 2026 - DREF Operation (MDRBO023) Format Situation Report Source IFRC Posted 26 Nov 2026 Originally published 25 Nov 2026 Argentina Argentina: Landslide - DREF Final Report (MDRAR025) Format Situation Report Source IFRC Posted 26 Nov 2026 Originally published 25 Nov 2026 DR Congo Rapport de la situation épidémiologique du choléra en RD Congo (Interne OMS), semaine 45, 2026 Format Situation Report Source WHO Posted 26 Nov 2026 Originally published 26 Nov 2026 Blog Labs About Us Terms Contact Facebook X LinkedIn OCHA Services Related Platforms Humanitarian Action Central Emergency Response Fund Other OCHA Services Financial Tracking Service Humanitarian Data Exchange ReliefWeb Response Inter-Agency Standing Committee OCHA website ReliefWeb Virtual OSOCC More OCHA Services Opens in a new window Service provided by United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs UN OCHA United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs OCHA coordinates the global emergency response to save lives and protect people in humanitarian crises. somalia.summary: The Somalia Weekly Weather Forecast for the period of November 25 to December 1, 2026, indicates a very dry week across the country. During the previous week (November 17-23), only four weather stations reported rainfall, with Banderbeyla recording the highest at 28.3 mm. Satellite estimates showed minimal precipitation in other areas, particularly in the river catchments of Ethiopia. Seasonal rainfall totals remain largely unchanged, with 37 stations having met their Deyr normal, including Baidoa and Galkacyo, which exceeded their averages significantly. However, Mogadishu and several other locations remain below their normal levels. River levels are decreasing, with major rivers well below flood-risk thresholds, particularly in Belet Weyne, where levels have dropped significantly. Flood waters in Jowhar district are receding, with satellite imagery showing a reduction in flooded areas. Reports from local callers indicate mixed reactions to the rainfall, with some areas experiencing flooding while others welcomed the moisture.

somalia.title: Somalia’s real problem is at home, not elsewhere - Gulf News
somalia.content: Somalia’s Internal Struggles: Why Blaming the UAE Won’t Solve the Crisis DUBAI 23°C GOLD/FOREX PRAYER TIMES NEWSLETTERS EPAPER GOLD/FOREX DUBAI 23°C PRAYER TIMES OPINION OPINION COLUMNISTS Opinion / Op-Eds Somalia’s real problem is at home, not elsewhere The country’s longstanding political disputes predate the latest diplomatic confrontation Last updated: November 26, 2026 | 06:46 Abdulaziz Ahmed Alshehhi , Special to Gulf News 5 MIN READ Add as a preferred source on Google According to the UAE’s 2022 foreign aid report, Somalia was the second-largest recipient of Emirati emergency food assistance that year. AP On November 19, the Somali government’s cabinet ordered the UAE’s ambassador to leave the country within 72 hours. The UAE’s involvement in Somalia has been described by Somali authorities as an “open invasion,” with action threatened against anyone who works with the UAE. These are serious accusations. However, when the facts are examined, what transpired over the past year tells a different story. It seems that this is a government that, rather than confronting its domestic challenges, has chosen to look outward for someone to blame. The timeline is the first step. The UAE Ministry of Foreign Affairs confirmed the closure of its embassy in Mogadishu and the withdrawal of its diplomatic personnel in January 2026. The Somali government subsequently ended its commercial, defence and security cooperation with the UAE. In truth, there was hardly any diplomatic activity left to terminate by November. Mogadishu’s decision came nearly ten months after diplomatic engagement had already been effectively suspended. Also Read: Anwar Gargash criticises Somali president's attack on UAE, reaffirms ties with its people What struck me was the calmness with which the UAE responded. The ministry condemned the Somali government’s escalatory and hostile attitude and expressed disappointment over its attempts to draw bilateral relations into Somalia’s internal political conflicts. The UAE also reaffirmed its longstanding respect for the Somali people in the same statement. No country seeking confrontation would respond in such a manner. Where is the real problem? So, where does the real problem lie? The answer lies within Somalia itself. President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud has been advocating constitutional and electoral reforms to give the federal government increased power, while several regions are vehemently opposing them. Puntland, however, has refused to follow Mogadishu’s lead, and federal forces have been expelled from Puntland. Federal troops have not succeeded in ejecting the regional leader in Jubaland following the controversial election in 2024. Since 1991, Somaliland has governed itself independently of Mogadishu’s authority. None of these disputes stem from the feud with the UAE; they all stem from a long-standing unresolved issue regarding the sharing of powers between the centre and the regions. Also Read: UAE strongly condemns Somalia's hostile approach, warns of damage to bilateral ties Blaming the UAE for all of this may be politically convenient, but not convincing. The leaders of Puntland hold an opposing view to Mogadishu because they believe the federal government has taken too much of their power, and with or without Abu Dhabi’s involvement, their stance would not differ. In January, Somaliland, Puntland and Jubaland all refused to comply with Mogadishu’s decision to cancel its agreements with the UAE, exercising their own political decision-making. Their independent political decisions should not automatically be interpreted as evidence that they are acting as foreign proxies. Such accusations also enable the federal government to turn a domestic political issue into a question of sovereignty, where anyone who disagrees can be accused of supporting an “invader,” despite the UAE’s longstanding humanitarian and developmental contributions through established legal channels. In his remarks, Dr Anwar Gargash, the UAE President’s diplomatic adviser, expressed similar concerns. He expressed concern that the Somali president’s accusations against the UAE reflect personal political motivations taking precedence over national interests. A leader facing considerable domestic challenges might seek an external adversary, but that is hardly beneficial for a nation that remains heavily reliant on international partners and allies. The UAE is not alone in putting forth this position. Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) Secretary-General, Ambassador Dr Jasem Mohamed Albudaiwi, criticised Somali officials for their “irresponsible” remarks and described the media campaign against the UAE as deceptive. He stated that these accusations undermined the UAE’s efforts to promote regional and international dialogue, while recognising its contributions to regional security and stability. That is a statement from the head of the six-member Gulf body. Long record of contribution The UAE’s longstanding record of contributions to Somalia constitutes one of the strongest arguments in its defence. In 2014, it opened its embassy in Mogadishu, the capital going through dangerous times and a war-torn nation. It funded a military training centre to support the development of a professional Somali army, and President Mohamud himself inaugurated that training centre in 2015. It also aided in the establishment of the Puntland Maritime Police Force, which has since developed into a front-line counterterrorism unit. In addition, the UAE has supported the fight against Al Shabaab Al Mujahideen and the Islamic State, and it is the Al Shabaab terrorist group and ISIS-Somalia that pose a significant threat to Somalia’s sovereignty. Humanitarian assistance is equally important. Years of insufficient rainfall and recurring droughts in Somalia prompted the UAE to take action by dispatching numerous relief ships and flights to the country through the Emirates Red Crescent and the Khalifa bin Zayed Al Nahyan Foundation, sometimes in cooperation with Somali humanitarian and disaster management authorities. The UAE also called for global attention and humanitarian assistance through the United Nations and other international platforms and institutions, showcasing its transparency in this regard. According to the UAE’s 2022 foreign aid report, Somalia was the second-largest recipient of Emirati emergency food assistance that year. In response to droughts, floods and conflicts, more than 700 tonnes of food were sent to affected families in early 2025. Assistance was extended to communities regardless of which local authorities governed them, including those in the Hiran region, Jubaland and Mogadishu. The ports developed through Emirati investment in Berbera and Bosaso have also generated significant economic and trade benefits for Somali communities. Projects to create opportunities Of course, any government has the right to review its agreements with another country. However, reviewing an agreement is a far cry from suddenly labelling a long-standing partner’s involvement as an “invasion,” particularly when the country’s own leadership was present at some of the project inaugurations, aware of the benefits they would bring and the genuine intentions behind them. These projects were designed to create mutually beneficial opportunities for both investors and the Somali people. After years of assistance delivered through proper channels, one can understand the disappointment expressed by Dr Anwar Gargash, particularly when such accusations are directed against a country that has provided Somali families with food and worked to combat terrorist groups. The UAE’s relationship with the Somali people will transcend these political disputes, and I believe the UAE will continue to adopt this wise stance. Effective diplomacy requires patience and the ability to distinguish between the political rhetoric of a government, its genuine understanding of the situation and the sincere beliefs of its people. Abu Dhabi remains open to the opportunity of restoring relations. It is now up to Mogadishu to decide whether to seize that opportunity or continue targeting foreign nations instead of addressing its domestic political disputes. somalia.summary: The recent diplomatic tensions between Somalia and the UAE have highlighted Somalia's internal political struggles rather than external influences. Following the Somali government's order for the UAE ambassador to leave, accusations of "open invasion" were made against the UAE. However, these claims appear to be a distraction from Somalia's longstanding issues, such as power-sharing disputes among its regions. President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud's push for reforms has faced resistance from regions like Puntland and Jubaland, which feel their autonomy is threatened. The UAE has been a significant humanitarian and developmental partner for Somalia, providing emergency aid and supporting military training. Critics argue that blaming the UAE is politically convenient for Somali leaders facing domestic challenges. The UAE’s calm response to the accusations reflects its commitment to the Somali people, emphasizing the need for Somalia to address its internal issues rather than deflecting blame onto foreign nations. Effective diplomacy requires recognizing the difference between political rhetoric and genuine national interests. (160 words)

somalia.title: Bitcoin drops below $56,000: Why a stronger U.S. dollar matters to Somalia - Hiiraan Online
somalia.content: Bitcoin drops below $56,000: Why a stronger U.S. dollar matters to Somalia - Hiiraan Online Jobs | Twitter | Somali Links | RSS Dark Mode Hiiraan Online HOME OPINION POLITICS RSS CONTACT US FACEBOOK × OPINION WARARKA MAANTA SPORTS SECURITY POLITICS Privacy Policy Contact Us Jobs advertisements HOME NEWS Bitcoin drops below $56,000: Why a stronger U.S. dollar matters to Somalia Share Facebook Messenger Twitter WhatsApp LinkedIn Telegram Copy Link Email Font Size A- A A+ Sunday November 22, 2026 Mogadishu (HOL) — Bitcoin briefly fell below $56,000 on Saturday, Nov. 21, hitting its lowest level in more than two years as a stronger U.S. dollar and uncertainty over American interest rates weighed on cryptocurrency markets. The world's largest cryptocurrency dropped to approximately $55,000 before recovering toward $60,000 later in the day. The decline left Bitcoin more than 50% below its October 2025 peak of over $126,000. advertisements For most Somali households, however, the cryptocurrency selloff has little direct effect on everyday spending. Commerce in Mogadishu, Hargeisa and other major cities relies heavily on U.S. dollars transferred through mobile money services rather than Bitcoin. The more immediate concern is the strengthening U.S. dollar, which can increase the cost of sending remittances for Somali workers earning their incomes in other currencies. Bitcoin's latest decline comes amid growing uncertainty in international financial markets over U.S. interest rates, inflation and the outlook for economic growth. Investors have reassessed expectations for Federal Reserve monetary policy, contributing to a stronger dollar and increasing pressure on risk-sensitive assets, including cryptocurrencies and technology stocks. The U.S. Dollar Index, which measures the dollar against a basket of major currencies, approached 104 during the week, reportedly its highest level in approximately 19 months. A stronger dollar can make dollar-denominated investments more expensive for international investors, while expectations of higher interest rates can increase the attractiveness of cash and government bonds relative to speculative assets. Bitcoin has also faced selling pressure from institutional investors, including funds holding the cryptocurrency through exchange-traded products. Institutional selling, combined with the forced liquidation of leveraged trading positions, has contributed to sharp price movements. The latest selloff highlights Bitcoin's continued vulnerability to changes in global financial conditions, despite its frequent promotion as a digital alternative to traditional stores of value. Somalia is among the economies most dependent on remittances from citizens living and working abroad. According to the Central Bank of Somalia's 2025 annual report, individual remittances reached $3.13 billion, up from $2.72 billion in 2024. These transfers represented approximately 24% of Somalia's gross domestic product in 2025, demonstrating their importance to household consumption and economic stability. Remittances help families pay for food, housing, education, healthcare and other basic necessities. Unlike countries where households primarily use domestic currencies, Somalia's economy is heavily dollarized. Many consumers receive, store and spend U.S. dollars through mobile money platforms such as EVC Plus, Zaad and Sahal. This system means changes in the dollar's international value can directly affect the cost of remittances for Somali workers living abroad. For example, a Somali worker in London earning British pounds must convert those earnings into U.S. dollars before sending money home. If the pound falls from $1.35 to $1.31, sending $200 would cost approximately £153 instead of £148, excluding transfer fees. The difference may appear modest for a single transaction, but repeated monthly transfers can become more expensive for workers supporting relatives in Somalia. The same pressure affects Somali workers earning euros, Canadian dollars and other currencies that weaken against the U.S. dollar. A stronger dollar does not necessarily reduce the amount received by a family in Somalia if the sender continues transferring the same dollar amount. Instead, it increases the cost for senders earning weaker foreign currencies. Somalia's reliance on the U.S. dollar provides some protection against exchange-rate instability compared with economies that depend on rapidly depreciating domestic currencies. However, dollarization does not shield households from inflation or increases in international commodity prices. Somalia imports substantial quantities of food, fuel, construction materials and manufactured goods, making domestic prices sensitive to changes in global supply chains, transportation costs and commodity markets. Rising energy prices, shipping disruptions and supply shortages can increase the cost of imported products, even when transactions are conducted in dollars. A stronger dollar can also reduce the dollar cost of goods priced in weaker foreign currencies, meaning its effect on Somalia's import bill depends on the product, supplier and market conditions. According to the International Monetary Fund's October 2026 assessment, Somalia's inflation rate is projected to reach 6.5% in 2026. Higher living costs, combined with pressure on remittance senders abroad, could place additional financial strain on households already facing economic and humanitarian challenges. Families that depend on regular financial assistance from relatives overseas may be particularly vulnerable if senders reduce the frequency or value of transfers because of unfavorable exchange rates. Although Bitcoin remains a speculative investment for many traders, dollar-pegged stablecoins such as USDT serve a different purpose. Stablecoins are cryptocurrencies designed to maintain a value linked to an underlying asset, usually the U.S. dollar. Some Somali freelancers and cross-border traders use stablecoins to transfer funds internationally without relying entirely on traditional banking channels. However, stablecoins carry their own risks, including issuer, liquidity, regulatory and technical risks, and their dollar pegs are not guaranteed. For most Somali households, conventional remittance companies and mobile money services remain more relevant than cryptocurrency markets. Bitcoin's decline illustrates how global financial markets react to changing expectations about interest rates, inflation and the strength of the U.S. dollar. A stronger dollar can increase the international purchasing power of dollar holdings, but it can also make dollar-denominated remittances more expensive for relatives earning income in other currencies. somalia.summary: Bitcoin recently fell below $56,000, marking its lowest point in over two years, primarily due to a stronger U.S. dollar and uncertainties surrounding American interest rates. This decline left Bitcoin over 50% lower than its peak in October 2025. While the cryptocurrency's volatility impacts global markets, it has minimal direct effects on everyday spending in Somalia, where commerce relies more on U.S. dollars transferred via mobile money services. The strengthening dollar increases remittance costs for Somali workers earning in weaker currencies, which can strain families dependent on these funds. In 2025, remittances accounted for about 24% of Somalia's GDP, highlighting their significance for household consumption. Although Bitcoin is viewed as a speculative asset, stablecoins linked to the dollar are used by some Somali traders for international transactions. However, traditional remittance methods remain more relevant for most households, as they navigate the challenges posed by inflation and rising living costs.

somalia.title: As foreign troops withdraw from Somalia, could al-Shabab take over? - BBC
somalia.content: As foreign troops withdraw from Somalia, could al-Shabab take over? Skip to content Watch Live British Broadcasting Corporation Home News Sport Business Technology Health Culture Arts Travel Earth Audio Video Live Documentaries Site search Home News Sport Business Technology Health Culture Arts Travel Earth Audio Video Live Documentaries Weather Newsletters Watch Live As foreign troops withdraw from Somalia, could al-Shabab take over? 3 hours ago Share Save Add as preferred on Google Basillioh Rukanga AFP via Getty Images Some analysts fear Somali security forces may not be able to handle the nation's security without external support Somalia is facing a fresh test of its stability as foreign troops begin withdrawing, funding for its security forces comes under pressure and a bitter political dispute threatens to derail plans for the country's first direct democratic elections in decades. The combination of challenges has raised questions about whether the government can defend itself against Islamist militant group al-Shabab while managing growing divisions among political factions. Some analysts fear the situation could embolden al-Shabab, which is affiliated with al-Qaeda, and potentially allow it to seize control of the capital, Mogadishu. The group already controls large parts of the country despite the presence of about 12,000 African Union (AU) troops supporting the government. The withdrawal of foreign forces, alongside the activities of clan-based militias aligned with rival political factions, has heightened concerns about the government's ability to maintain control. Ugandan troops, who make up the largest contingent of the AU force, began withdrawing last month, with the country expected to complete its withdrawal by next year. Ethiopia, another major contributor to the AU mission, is also reportedly planning to withdraw about 3,000 troops. The country has 2,500 troops authorised under the AU mission and roughly 5,000 under a bilateral agreement with Somalia. It is not clear whether the reported withdrawals would be from the AU contingent, the bilateral force, or both. The US, which had earlier announced cuts to funding for the UN Support Office in Somalia (UNSOS) has since said it is extending it for a year. Washington contributes about a quarter of $500m UNSOS's annual budget, which supports Somali security forces, AU missions and individual troop-contributing nations. With military support uncertain and the government facing mounting political challenges, analysts question whether Somalia's security forces are ready to stand on their own. The concerns were heightened recently when al-Shabab claimed to have killed hundreds of elite Somali soldiers in an attack. The government acknowledged the attack but did not disclose the number of casualties. Abdisalam Guleid, a former deputy director of Somalia's National Security Agency, told the BBC the security situation was increasingly precarious. He warned that the withdrawal of foreign troops could leave Mogadishu vulnerable to a takeover similar to that of Afghanistan by the Taliban in 2021, following the withdrawal of US and Nato forces. "I don't think Mogadishu will be able to defend itself. The Taliban style [takeover]… that's the most likely scenario I can envision now," he said. The Taliban took over control of Afghanistan between 6-15 August 2021 in a rapid offensive, following the withdrawal of US and NATO forces. Such a scenario has played out in Somalia in the past, Guleid explains. Why is Uganda fighting in 'hellish' Somalia? Somalia has experienced the collapse of central authority before. In the early 1990s, clan-based rebel groups advanced on Mogadishu from several fronts, forcing then-President Mohamed Siad Barre from power. His overthrow triggered a devastating civil war and a prolonged humanitarian crisis. The collapse of state institutions subsequently created conditions in which Islamist militant groups, including al-Shabab, were able to expand their influence. Guleid says Ugandan troops have been central to preventing a similar collapse since their first deployment to Somalia in 2007. They played a key role in driving al-Shabab out of Mogadishu and other major towns, while protecting strategic installations, including the airport, seaport, government institutions and diplomatic missions. Troops from Burundi, Djibouti, Kenya, Sierra Leone and Ethiopia later joined the AU mission, while countries including Turkey and the US maintained separate military deployments and provided training and equipment to Somali forces. But Guleid argues that years of international assistance have not translated into sufficient military independence for the Somali government. He says the authorities have become so reliant on foreign protection that they have neglected to adequately prepare their own forces to take over. Somalia's Information Minister Abdifatah Qasim Mohamud rejected suggestions that the country would be unable to cope with the withdrawals. He told the BBC that Somali troops had already taken over some positions vacated by Ugandan forces and were prepared to assume greater responsibility for the country's security. He said Somalia could not depend indefinitely on foreign troops for its protection. "I believe there is no reason for concern over this issue. There will be no change in the country's security situation or in the areas they have vacated," he said. President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud has also been seeking continued international backing. During a visit to Uganda on 23 November, he and President Yoweri Museveni called on the international community to continue supporting Somalia to consolidate security gains. Getty Images Uganda troops were first deployed to Somalia in 2007 Not everyone believes the withdrawal will necessarily result in a security collapse. Ugandan security analyst Freddie David Egesa argues that years of international military support have helped Somalia establish the institutions needed to take greater responsibility for its security. He says the withdrawal will provide an opportunity to assess how much progress has been made. It will also force Somalia's political leaders to put aside their differences and take greater responsibility for the country's future, he adds. But other analysts warn that the timing could hardly be worse. Omar Mahmood, an analyst at the International Crisis Group, says Somali forces are under considerable pressure as they fight al-Shabab while attempting to take over positions previously held by foreign troops. This is a major undertaking for an army that is still developing, he says. The military is also facing pressure in the Bay region of the South-West state, where forces loyal to ousted regional President Abdiaziz Hassan Mohamed have been fighting the federal government. The withdrawal of Ugandan troops from the Lower Shabelle region could create further security challenges, Mahmood adds. Mahmood further points to the long-delayed elections, which need to be secured, as another issue compounding the security situation. Somalia has been attempting to move away from an indirect electoral system in which clan elders select lawmakers, who then elect the president, towards a system of direct voting. Beyond the military situation, Mahmood says, the government must also resolve a growing political dispute over the timing and format of the country's elections. But the proposed changes have divided the government and opposition, with disagreements over how the elections should be conducted. The dispute escalated this year after Mohamud pushed through constitutional amendments extending the presidential term from four to five years, effectively delaying the next elections until 2027. AFP via Getty Images Al-Shabab militants still pose a big threat against the government This month, the Supreme Court ruled against the extension, ordering political leaders to agree on an electoral roadmap within 30 days and to hold elections within three months. A day before the ruling, Mohamud dismissed Chief Justice Baashe Yusuf Ahmed. He and other judges in the case have filed a suit against Somalia over the dismissals at the East African regional court in Tanzania. The Somali government has since rejected the Supreme Court's decision, with its implementation now uncertain. Mahmood says the political and security crises are closely connected, with the absence of consensus over the elections making it harder for the government to focus on the fight against al-Shabab. Guleid also warns that the threat to Somalia's stability comes not only from the militant group but from clan-based militias increasingly challenging the federal government. "Today, we have clan loyalists fighting alongside al-Shabab against the federal government," he said. He added the country's leadership appears unable to anticipate the scale of the challenges ahead. Who will fill the gap left by foreign partners? Somalia's security challenges are compounded by its heavy dependence on international financial support. Latest data from its finance ministry shows that donor grants amounting to $878.8m accounts for two-thirds of its planned $1.36bn budget in 2026. Despite that, the ministry said it had only received about $314m of grants in the first nine months of the year, equivalent to 35% the expected annual aid. Mahmood believes that although some international military support is declining, other partners could help bridge the gap through bilateral agreements and continued assistance. But Guleid is sceptical that countries such as Turkey, Qatar and Egypt could quickly replace the military and financial contributions of Uganda and the US. He argues that Somalia's dependence on external support makes it particularly vulnerable when international partners change their priorities. That dependence has also contributed to increasingly strained relations with some foreign governments. Anadolu via Getty Images Somalia's challenges are compounded by its heavy reliance on foreign support Somalia has accused the United Arab Emirates of funding armed groups and undermining its sovereignty, in the latest dispute involving an external power with significant security and economic interests in the country. The UAE has rejected the criticism and hit back at the Somali leader, describing him as an "outgoing president" in reference to the dispute over his presidential mandate. The two countries formally severed ties earlier this year, although the UAE has long been an important security and economic partner in Somalia. The dispute illustrates the difficult relationship Somalia has with foreign partners on whom it relies for security, funding and political support. For Egesa, the withdrawal of foreign troops could ultimately provide an opportunity for Somalia to demonstrate how much progress it has made in rebuilding its security institutions. He believes the staggered departure of troops will allow Somali forces to assume responsibility gradually, while also forcing rival political factions to work together. But Guleid remains far less optimistic. He argues that unless Somalia addresses its military weaknesses, political divisions and growing influence of armed groups, it risks losing the security gains made. For now, it faces the difficult task of fighting an entrenched insurgency, managing rival political interests and preparing for a contentious electoral process, all while some of military partners are preparing to leave. Whether Somalia can withstand these pressures without renewed instability remains an open question. The combination of challenges has raised questions about whether the government can defend itself against Islamist militant group al-Shabab while managing growing divisions among political factions. Some analysts fear the situation could embolden al-Shabab, which is affiliated with al-Qaeda, and potentially allow it to seize control of the capital, Mogadishu. The group already controls large parts of the country despite the presence of about 12,000 African Union (AU) troops supporting the government. The withdrawal of foreign forces, alongside the activities of clan-based militias aligned with rival political factions, has heightened concerns about the government's ability to maintain control. Ugandan troops, who make up the largest contingent of the AU force, began withdrawing last month, with the country expected to complete its withdrawal by next year. Ethiopia, another major contributor to the AU mission, is also reportedly planning to withdraw about 3,000 troops. The country has 2,500 troops authorised under the AU mission and roughly 5,000 under a bilateral agreement with Somalia. It is not clear whether the reported withdrawals would be from the AU contingent, the bilateral force, or both. The US, which had earlier announced cuts to funding for the UN Support Office in Somalia (UNSOS) has since said it is extending it for a year. Washington contributes about a quarter of $500m UNSOS's annual budget, which supports Somali security forces, AU missions and individual troop-contributing nations. With military support uncertain and the government facing mounting political challenges, analysts question whether Somalia's security forces are ready to stand on their own. The concerns were heightened recently when al-Shabab claimed to have killed hundreds of elite Somali soldiers in an attack. The government acknowledged the attack but did not disclose the number of casualties. Abdisalam Guleid, a former deputy director of Somalia's National Security Agency, told the BBC the security situation was increasingly precarious. He warned that the withdrawal of foreign troops could leave Mogadishu vulnerable to a takeover similar to that of Afghanistan by the Taliban in 2021, following the withdrawal of US and Nato forces. "I don't think Mogadishu will be able to defend itself. The Taliban style [takeover]… that's the most likely scenario I can envision now," he said. The Taliban took over control of Afghanistan between 6-15 August 2021 in a rapid offensive, following the withdrawal of US and NATO forces. Such a scenario has played out in Somalia in the past, Guleid explains. Why is Uganda fighting in 'hellish' Somalia? In the early 1990s, clan-based rebel groups advanced on Mogadishu from several fronts, forcing then-President Mohamed Siad Barre from power. He says the authorities have become so reliant on foreign protection that they have neglected to adequately prepare their own forces to take over. He told the BBC that Somali troops had already taken over some positions vacated by Ugandan forces and were prepared to assume greater responsibility for the country's security. Spanning clinical records from January 2022 through July 2026, the investigation monitored 490 patients of all ages, providing the first comprehensive clinical assessment of osteomyelitis presentations, microbiological profiles, and therapeutic results within the Somali tertiary healthcare system. Demographic and clinical evaluations demonstrated that the condition disproportionately affected young patients and males throughout the studied population. Among the 490 recorded individuals, 339 patients, representing 69.2 percent of the cohort, were male, while 244 patients, or 49.8 percent, were younger than 18 years of age. The clinical presentation was overwhelmingly non-acute, with chronic osteomyelitis documented in 66.1 percent of all cases. Furthermore, 63.9 percent of the infections developed secondary to physical trauma, and anatomical assessments identified the tibia as the single most frequently compromised skeletal site, accounting for 39.6 percent of the localized bone infections reviewed by the clinical team. Treatment modalities varied across the cohort between combined surgical management and non-operative pharmacological intervention. Operative procedures were undertaken in 336 patients, constituting 68.6 percent of the clinical population, while the remaining 154 patients received antibiotic regimens without surgical debridement or operative measures. The authors observed a median follow-up duration of six months among the participants, although individual antibiotic regimens and administration parameters were not systematically documented in the institutional records. Microbiological assessments identified viable bacterial pathogens in 306 out of 485 patients who underwent diagnostic testing, yielding an overall culture positivity rate of 63.1 percent. Staphylococcus aureus emerged as the predominant causative organism, isolated in 59.2 percent of the culture-positive cases. Within these staphylococcal isolates, 27.1 percent were confirmed to be methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus. Patient outcomes were recorded for 448 individuals at their last documented clinical visit, with treatment failure defined as recurrence, persistent infection, or required amputation. Overall, 200 patients, representing 44.6 percent of those with known outcomes, experienced an unfavourable result at their final evaluation. However, among a subgroup of patients who were actively monitored for at least six months, the proportion of unfavourable outcomes dropped to 23.4 percent. The researchers noted that because overall follow-up was relatively short, the precise proportion of individuals whose bone infections remained uncontrolled over extended periods could not be determined with complete certainty. To identify independent risk factors governing clinical failure, the investigators performed multivariable Firth penalized logistic regression alongside multiple sensitivity analyses. Gram-negative bacterial organisms were also strongly associated with poor outcomes, demonstrating an adjusted odds ratio of 4.37 and a 95 percent confidence interval of 2.27 to 8.59. These specific pathogen associations maintained statistical significance throughout every conducted sensitivity analysis. The multivariable regression models further highlighted the influence of host demographic and inflammatory markers on treatment success. Each additional ten years of patient age was linked to an elevated risk of clinical failure, corresponding to an adjusted odds ratio of 1.17 with a 95 percent confidence interval between 1.05 and 1.30. In addition, higher baseline systemic inflammation, measured through serum C-reactive protein, predicted worse clinical results, showing an adjusted odds ratio of 1.06 per ten milligram per liter increase, with a 95 percent confidence interval of 1.03 to 1.10. Based on these findings, the authors concluded that osteomyelitis in this Somali medical center primarily burdens pediatric patients and young men suffering from post-traumatic lower-limb injuries. Finally, the investigators urged the medical community to initiate prospective observational studies featuring comprehensive antibiotic logging and prolonged clinical follow-up to validate these retrospective findings. somalia.summary: A retrospective cohort study conducted at a tertiary care hospital in Mogadishu, Somalia, has found a significant association between methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) and Gram-negative pathogens with poor outcomes in osteomyelitis patients. Analyzing clinical records from January 2022 to July 2026, the study included 490 patients, predominantly young males, with chronic osteomyelitis being the most common presentation. The tibia was the most affected site, and 63.9% of infections were linked to physical trauma. Treatment varied, with 68.6% undergoing surgical intervention. Of the 448 patients with recorded outcomes, 44.6% experienced treatment failure. Notably, Gram-negative bacteria were linked to a fourfold increase in the risk of poor outcomes. The study emphasizes the need for further research, including prospective studies with comprehensive antibiotic tracking, to validate these findings and improve treatment strategies for osteomyelitis in Somalia.

somalia.title: Somalia dismisses security vacuum fears as Ugandan troops withdraw - Hiiraan Online
somalia.content: Somalia dismisses security vacuum fears as Ugandan troops withdraw - Hiiraan Online Jobs | Twitter | Somali Links | RSS Dark Mode Hiiraan Online HOME OPINION POLITICS RSS CONTACT US FACEBOOK × OPINION WARARKA MAANTA SPORTS SECURITY POLITICS Privacy Policy Contact Us Jobs advertisements HOME SECURITY Somalia dismisses security vacuum fears as Ugandan troops withdraw Share Facebook Messenger Twitter WhatsApp LinkedIn Telegram Copy Link Email Font Size A- A A+ Sunday November 22, 2026 Mogadishu (HOL) — Somali federal government has dismissed concerns that the withdrawal of Ugandan troops could create a security vacuum, insisting that the Somali National Army is prepared to take over positions vacated by foreign forces. Speaking during a BBC Somali debate on Friday, Information Minister Abdifatah Qasim Mohamud said the government had spent recent years strengthening and training its armed forces, including soldiers who recently returned from military training abroad. He said Ugandan troops had already handed over some of their positions directly to Somali forces as part of the ongoing security transition. advertisements "We have no concerns that this will negatively impact the country's security situation or the areas vacated by these troops," Abdifatah said. The minister emphasized that foreign troops were deployed to Somalia for specific missions and limited periods, arguing that their departure should not be interpreted as evidence that Somalia lacks the military capacity to protect itself. He said Somalia's security could not remain permanently dependent on international peacekeeping forces and that the government was committed to assuming full responsibility for national security. His remarks follow Uganda's announcement earlier this month that it had begun withdrawing troops deployed under bilateral security arrangements with Somalia. The Uganda People's Defence Forces (UPDF) said the withdrawal would be conducted in phases, with all Ugandan troops, including those serving under the African Union Support and Stabilization Mission in Somalia (AUSSOM), expected to leave by the end of 2027. Uganda has been one of the largest contributors to African Union peacekeeping operations in Somalia since 2007, with its forces playing a major role in securing Mogadishu and supporting military operations against al-Shabab. The planned withdrawal has raised concerns among some security officials and lawmakers about the readiness of Somali forces to assume responsibility for strategic locations previously protected by Ugandan troops. Abdifatah specifically challenged comments made by lawmaker Kooshin during a BBC Somali discussion, in which the MP reportedly warned that Somalia was not yet prepared to take full control of areas vacated by Ugandan peacekeepers. Kooshin argued that security in Mogadishu and parts of Lower Shabelle and Middle Shabelle remained dependent on African Union forces. Responding to the criticism, the information minister questioned whether areas that had previously fallen under al-Shabab control had been liberated exclusively by Somali troops or with the support of international peacekeepers. He maintained that the Somali National Army had played the leading role in liberating several areas from the militant group, citing military operations between Mogadishu and Harardhere as examples. Abdifatah said the federal government had made significant investments in military training and capacity-building over the past five years to prepare national forces for greater security responsibilities. However, concerns about the withdrawal have also been raised by international security officials. In a report earlier this month, Reuters cited an African Union communication warning that the departure of Ugandan forces could leave parts of Lower Shabelle vulnerable to attacks by al-Shabab. Somalia's State Minister for Foreign Affairs, Ali Mohamed Omar, also previously acknowledged that a sudden withdrawal could create security problems, although he said the situation was not immediately critical. The differing assessments reflect continued debate over Somalia's readiness to complete the security transition as African Union troop-contributing countries review their deployments and international funding remains uncertain. Al-Shabab, an al-Qaeda-linked militant group, continues to carry out attacks against Somali security forces and maintains a presence in parts of southern and central Somalia. Despite these concerns, Abdifatah reiterated that the government was confident in the national army's ability to assume greater security responsibilities as Ugandan and other foreign troops gradually withdraw.
